studies.title: A Victory No One Could See
studies.meaning: A treaty that looked to the companions like a humbling climb-down is named a clear victory. The naming comes first, before any explanation. Four things follow, joined in one chain: forgiveness, the completing of a favour, guidance on a straight path, and unwavering support. Scholars differ over which opening is meant. Most read it as the truce made outside Mecca. Some read it as the later entry into the city itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the sixth year after the emigration. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had set out for the pilgrimage with about fourteen hundred unarmed men. He was stopped at Hudaybiyyah, outside Mecca. A treaty was agreed there on terms the companions found bitter: they would turn back that year and return the next. The surah came down on the journey home. The classical sources are unusually detailed about the occasion.

keyTerms.note: The root means to open, a door, a lock, a sealed thing. Calling a treaty an opening is exact rather than generous: what the truce opened was free travel and conversation between two sides previously at war.
A participle from a verb meaning both to be clear and to make clear. The word insists the victory is visible, which is the point of contention: nobody present could see it yet.
From a root for what is rare, hard and unassailable, the same root behind one of God's names. Applied to help, it means aid that cannot be pushed back rather than aid that is merely large.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A treaty between tribes in Arabia was a public, memorised thing. There was no archive; the terms lived in the memory of the witnesses and in the reputation of whoever signed. Breaking one was a matter of honour rather than law, which is why terms that looked one-sided were felt as shame. Fourteen hundred men who had travelled in pilgrim dress, unarmed except for sheathed swords, turned around without reaching the House.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical sources preserve a report from the road back from the truce. The Prophet said a chapter had come down to him that was dearer to him than everything the sun rises upon. Then he recited this opening. Historians of the period note that more people entered the community in the two years after the truce than in all the years before it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows that naming an event is not the same as seeing it. And the naming comes from outside. What the companions could measure was a concession. What they were told was an opening. The forgiveness clause is placed as the purpose of the victory, not its reward. That reverses the expected order and makes the outcome a tool. Guidance and support are then described as still being completed, not finished.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same episode later in the surah and explains the delay, saying God knew what the community did not.
States as a principle what this passage states as an event, that judgement about a setback can be wrong.
Uses the same word for opening at the end of the mission, and answers it with praise and seeking pardon.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing from the past year that you filed as a loss. Write two lines: what it cost, and what it made possible that could not have happened otherwise. If the second line is empty, leave it empty and date the page. The companions did not see this victory on the day it was announced either.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet that he has been given a clear win. Because of it, God will forgive his wrongs, past and future. God will finish his kindness to him and guide him on a straight road. God will also give him strong help.

studies.title: Calm Sent Down From Outside
studies.meaning: Calm is described as something sent down, using the verb the Quran reserves for revelation and rain. It arrives from outside the person. Its stated effect is not comfort. It is an increase of faith on top of faith already there, which makes the calm a means rather than an end. The second half then names the armies of the heavens and the earth. So the steadiness inside a frightened man is set beside forces he cannot see.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It is part of the surah that came down on the road back from the truce agreed outside Mecca, in the sixth year after the emigration. The companions had been stopped short of the pilgrimage. They had accepted terms that felt like defeat. Several of them are described in the sources as openly distressed. This ayah names what held them at the moment they were being asked to turn around.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be still and to dwell. The same letters give the words for a home and for a knife. It names stillness that has come to rest, not the absence of fear.
The verb used of revelation, of rain and of iron. Calm belongs to that list rather than to the vocabulary of feeling, so it is treated as something delivered, not produced by effort.

The plain military word for an army. Using it of the heavens and the earth places angels, weather and circumstance in one category, and reminds a small band that the visible count of men is not the whole force.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fourteen hundred men were camped in a shallow valley a day's march from a city that had tried to kill them, without armour and without water enough to be comfortable. Rumours ran through a camp like that faster than orders. The negotiations took days, and men sat in the heat with nothing to do but talk. Anything that steadied a camp in those conditions was worth more than reinforcements.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for this calm occurs six times in the Quran. Three of those are in this one surah. Of the other three, one describes a chest carried by the Children of Israel. The other two describe moments when the Prophet's companions were badly outnumbered, or reduced to two men in a cave.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Inner states are usually where a person feels most in charge. This ayah puts one of them wholly outside human making. That has a consequence. Calm under pressure is not proof of strength of character. And its absence is not proof of weak faith. The passage also puts the unseen on the same footing as the seen. Whatever is felt in a heart and whatever stands in the sky are named as belonging to one owner.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word at the smallest possible scale, two men hidden in a cave with a search party outside.
Attaches the same calm to a physical object carried before an army, the earliest use of the word in the Quran's order.
Names a different verb for the settling of hearts and ties it to remembrance rather than to a moment of crisis.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are calm in a situation that should have rattled you, stop and mark it. Do not congratulate yourself on handling it well. This ayah describes that steadiness arriving from somewhere, and the practical difference is that you can ask for it in advance, which is not something you can do with your own composure.
studies.explainEasier: God sent calm down into the hearts of the believers, so their trust would grow even stronger. The armies of the sky and the earth belong to God. He knows what he is doing.

studies.title: The Purpose Clause
studies.meaning: This ayah is not a sentence of its own. It begins with a particle of purpose and completes a thought that started several ayat earlier, so what it supplies is the reason behind everything just described: the opening, the calm sent down, the promise of forgiveness. All of it is said to be for this. The reward is then given in two halves, an entry and a remission, and the second is placed after the first rather than before it. Believing men and believing women are named separately, which is a deliberate feature of this surah.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the surah revealed in connection with the agreement made at Hudaybiyyah, when a party travelling toward Mecca was turned back and accepted terms that many at the time found hard. The surah reframes that episode as an opening rather than a setback. This ayah belongs to the opening sequence, where the outcome of the whole affair is stated before any of its details are given.

keyTerms.note: The opening particle makes the whole ayah a purpose clause attached to what came before, so it reads as the reason for events rather than as a separate promise added after them.
Both forms are given rather than the masculine plural standing for everyone, which Arabic would allow. This surah does the same in the following ayah for the other side of the contrast.
A word for coming through safely and getting what was sought, used of a man who escapes danger and gains his object at once. It is the Quran's usual term for the final outcome.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The party that had set out toward Mecca had gone in a state of pilgrimage, unarmed except for travellers' swords, and expected either to enter the sanctuary or to be prevented. They were prevented. They shaved their heads and turned back at the boundary, having signed terms that included returning anyone who came over to them. Men wept. This ayah, and the surah around it, arrived on the road home.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase closing this ayah, a great attainment, appears three times in the Quran in exactly this form, and each time it is attached to something different: to a share of spoils being envied, to a life whose conduct has been set right, and here to entry and remission together. The same two words do very different work in each place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Making the reward a purpose clause changes how the events around it are read. What happened at the boundary is not presented as a setback later compensated, but as a step in something aimed at this from the start. The order inside the promise matters too. Entry is named before remission, so the pardon is described as arriving inside the destination rather than as the ticket that gets someone through the gate.

crossReferences.why: Begins the sentence this ayah completes, with the opening granted and the calm sent down.
Names believing men and women in parallel through an entire ayah, ten qualities each time.
Attaches the same promise of gardens to believing men and women, and adds God's approval as greater.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disappointment from a few years ago that you can now see the shape of. Not a lesson learned, the actual sequence: this happened, then that became possible. Write the two clauses down. The ayah is doing exactly that for its audience while they were still on the road home, which is much harder than doing it afterward.

studies.title: Thinking Ill Of God
studies.meaning: The other half of the purpose clause, and it identifies its subject by a thought rather than by a deed. Those described are people who assumed the worst about God, and the phrase names an evil assumption specifically, not doubt or ignorance. Then a turn of phrase that Arabic uses for fortune: the reversal they were waiting for is said to be on them. What follows is a sequence of consequences rather than an argument, and the ayah, like the one before it, names men and women separately in both categories.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The setting is the expedition toward Mecca and the agreement made at its edge. Some who stayed behind had reasoned that the party would not come back, and the surah addresses that calculation directly a few ayat later. The classical commentators read this ayah as describing the assumption behind the staying rather than the staying itself. No separate occasion is reported for it.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from a verb covering both supposition and near-certainty. What is criticised is not uncertainty but a settled assumption, and the ayah specifies which kind by the word that follows.

From the root for a circle: the wheel coming round. The phrase belongs to the vocabulary of expecting a reversal in someone else's affairs, and it appears twice in the Quran, both times of people waiting for one.
From a verb meaning to become. It names not merely a place arrived at but what a thing turns into, which makes the destination the outcome of a process rather than a sentence imposed at the end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian politics ran on reading which way things were going. Neutral clans watched a conflict and committed late, alliances were adjusted after a defeat, and men held back from a risky expedition while keeping their standing with both sides. Waiting for the wheel to turn was ordinary prudence, not treachery, in a world without written guarantees. The ayah takes that entirely reasonable calculation and describes what it assumes about God.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for waiting on a turn of fortune occurs twice in the Quran, and the other occurrence describes people among the desert Arabs who treated their contributions as a fine and waited for the wheel to come round against the believers. The two passages use the identical expression and hold it up in the same way, as a calculation rather than an accusation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats an assumption as a moral position, which is a strong claim. What a person quietly expects of God shapes every decision made under uncertainty, and it operates below the level of anything he would state. Naming men and women separately on both sides of this surah's contrast has an effect here too: the assumption being described is not a fault of one part of a community but a way of thinking available to anyone.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same phrase about waiting for the wheel to turn, in the same Medinan setting.
Describes the same assumption after a reverse: thinking about God what belonged to an older way of thinking.
Says the assumption people held about their Lord was itself what ruined them, and names it directly.

studies.applyIt: Catch the assumption you make when something goes wrong. Not the thing you would say if asked, the flicker before that: this always happens to me, it was never going to work. That flicker is a claim about how things are arranged. Name it once today, in words, and notice how little evidence it was carrying.

studies.title: Morning And Evening
studies.meaning: Three ayat move from the largest scale to the smallest. First a statement about forces belonging to God, repeated from a few ayat earlier, which places every visible strength inside something larger. Then the messenger's role in three words: a witness, a bringer of good news, a warner. Then the purpose, and it narrows to four verbs. Believe, support, honour, and glorify morning and evening. The commentators differ over which of the last three attach to God and which to the messenger, and record the readings without settling the question.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the opening section of the surah connected with the agreement at Hudaybiyyah. The party had gone out expecting one thing and come back with terms instead, and the surah's early ayat repeatedly relocate power away from what happened on the ground. Naming the forces of the heavens and the earth twice in four ayat belongs to that pattern. No specific occasion is reported for these three.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary military word for organised bodies of fighting men. Applying it to the heavens and the earth uses the vocabulary of the situation the audience was in and moves it to a scale they could not survey.
From the root for heaviness and dignity. It means to accord something its proper gravity rather than to praise it, and the verb occurs once in the Quran, in this ayah.
A fixed pair naming the two ends of the working day rather than exact hours. The phrase occurs four times in the Quran and marks the outer edges of a period, so it stands for its whole span.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A day in that climate was organised around its two cool ends. Animals were watered and moved at first light, work was done before the heat, and business resumed in the late afternoon until dark. Travellers set out early and made camp before dusk. Naming those two moments named the frame everyone's day already had, so an instruction attached to them did not require a new hour to be found in a full schedule.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the four verbs in the last of these ayat occur nowhere else in the Quran. One is the word for supporting or strengthening; the other is the word for treating something with due weight. They sit together in a single clause, and the commentators have long discussed which of the pronouns attached to them point to God and which to the messenger.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence puts remembrance at the end of a chain that begins with cosmic forces, which is an unexpected place to land. Having named armies that cannot be counted, the passage arrives at four things a person does, and the last of them is bounded by ordinary daylight. That implies a specific relation between scale and practice: what is asked of a human being is not proportionate to what is described about God, and is not meant to be.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same three-word description of the messenger's role, and adds a caller and a lamp.
Contains the identical clause about the forces of the heavens and the earth, four ayat earlier.
Attaches remembrance to the same two ends of the day, and asks that it be much rather than occasional.

studies.applyIt: Attach one short remembrance to something you already do at both ends of the day. The first time you sit down in the morning, the moment you get home. Do not add a slot to your schedule; the ayah names the edges of the day precisely because everyone already has them. Keep it for a week before deciding whether it works.

studies.title: A Hand Above Their Hands
studies.meaning: A pledge made by clasping hands is described as reaching past the person whose hand was taken. Then a phrase the classical commentators handle with care, saying that God's hand is above theirs and that no bodily hand is intended, while declining to reduce the expression to a bare metaphor. The rest is symmetry. Breaking the pledge is described as breaking it against oneself, which relocates the damage, and fulfilling it is answered with a reward left unspecified except in size.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the sources connect this ayah to the pledge given under a tree at Hudaybiyyah, when a rumour reached the camp that an envoy sent into Mecca had been killed. Those present pledged themselves one by one to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The pledge was given before it was known what would be required, and the agreement that followed changed the situation entirely.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a sale. Arabic uses the same word for a commercial transaction and for a pledge of loyalty, because both were concluded by striking hands, and the exchange is what the verb names.
To undo something twisted, as a rope is picked back into loose fibre. It names not a refusal to keep a promise but the coming apart of something that had been made whole.
To bring a thing to its full measure. It belongs with the words for completing a weight or discharging a debt, so keeping a covenant is described in the vocabulary of paying what is owed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agreements were made with hands, not documents. Two men clasped right hands in front of witnesses, and that gesture concluded a sale, a marriage arrangement or an oath of loyalty. There was no registry to appeal to afterward, so the whole weight rested on memory and on standing. A man who unpicked such a bond was known for it, and the knowledge travelled with him for the rest of his life.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase God's hand appears twice in the Quran. The other occurrence is quoted from opponents as something said in mockery, that His hand is fettered, and the Quran rejects it. Here the same two words are used affirmatively, placed above the hands of people making a pledge, and the classical commentators discuss the difference at length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah changes what a promise is by changing who receives it. If the pledge lands somewhere other than where the hand was placed, then its keeping cannot be adjusted by circumstances between the two human parties, and no later disappointment in the person pledged to releases it. The reversal in the middle then removes the usual motive for breaking one. There is nobody to get the better of, since the loss is described as falling on the one who unravels it.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same pledge a few ayat later and says God was pleased with those who gave it.
Uses the same image of unravelling, of a woman undoing thread she had spun into strong yarn.
Describes another exchange in the vocabulary of trade, and tells them to rejoice in the bargain struck.

studies.applyIt: Think of a commitment you made to someone who has since disappointed you, and notice how quickly that felt like a release. Sometimes it is. Often the disappointment is doing work the promise never gave it. Pick one small thing you said you would do and do it this week regardless of how the other person has behaved.

studies.title: Our Property Kept Us Busy
studies.meaning: The ayah reports a conversation before it happens, in the future tense, and quotes the excuse word for word. Property and family kept us occupied, so ask forgiveness for us. Nothing in that sentence is false; the excuse is plausible and probably even accurate. What the ayah adds is a gap between the tongue and what lies behind it, and the request for forgiveness is the part it identifies as hollow. The reply given does not argue with the excuse. It asks who could hold anything back from God on their behalf, either way.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The journey toward Mecca had looked likely to end badly, and groups from the surrounding desert who had been asked to come declined. The surah addresses them directly here and again a few ayat later. The classical sources treat the ayah as anticipating what would be said on the party's return, which is why the verb is in the future, and they report no separate occasion for it.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle: those who were left, not those who stayed. The form is faintly ironic, since the people described had made their own choice, and it appears three times in the Quran.
To be taken up with something, so that attention is used elsewhere. The verb does not claim inability, only that the capacity was in use, which is what makes the excuse hard to disprove.

The physical organ named separately from the heart in the same sentence. Arabic uses the word for language itself, so the phrase sets the mechanism of speech against the place speech is supposed to come from.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: For people living outside the towns, an absence of weeks was expensive in a way settled families could not always feel. Herds needed daily movement to water, a household without its men was exposed, and a season missed could not be recovered. The excuse quoted here is the true condition of desert life stated accurately. The ayah does not dispute the facts. It goes to the sentence attached at the end of them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for those left behind occurs three times in the Quran and every occurrence is in a Medinan surah about an expedition. In each place it takes the same passive form, describing people as having been left rather than as having stayed, which reverses the direction of the decision they had actually made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates an accurate statement from a truthful one. Everything said is defensible and the request appended to it is not, because the request is for something the speaker does not want. That makes sincerity a matter of what a sentence is for rather than of whether its contents are correct. The reply then removes the transaction entirely: no intermediary can adjust what God intends, so seeking one is answering a question nobody asked.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same group in an earlier expedition, glad to have stayed and disliking the effort.
Shows a similar request for intercession being declined, and says asking would make no difference.
Addresses desert Arabs again, distinguishing what they declared from what had actually entered their hearts.

studies.applyIt: Listen to your next apology as it leaves your mouth. Is it asking for something, or offering something. The excuse in this ayah is true and the request tacked on the end is doing the work. Try one apology this week with nothing attached, no explanation and no request, and notice how much harder it is to say.

studies.title: You Thought They Would Not Return
studies.meaning: The real reason is supplied in place of the excuse just quoted, and it is a forecast rather than a fault of character. You calculated that the party would never come back to their families. Then a second clause names what happened to that calculation: it was made to look attractive in the heart, so a piece of prudence became a preference. The word closing the first ayah names something spoiled past use. The second ayah widens from the specific group to a general statement, which is how the surah keeps returning from an episode to a principle.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Fourteen hundred people had set out toward a city that had been at war with them for years, in a state of pilgrimage and effectively unarmed. Estimating that they would not return was not cowardice but arithmetic, and the groups asked to join them made that estimate. The surah is addressing them after the party came back, having agreed terms at the boundary rather than fighting.

keyTerms.note: To be turned over or reversed, used of a traveller heading home and of something flipped. It is the ordinary word for coming back from a journey, which is what makes the never in the sentence so flat.
The passive with no agent named, the same construction used in the surah before this one. What is described is a forecast that stopped being neutral and started being wanted.
Used of land that has gone barren and of goods that have perished. As a standalone word it appears twice in the Quran, and both times it describes people rather than things.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone in that world could estimate the odds of a journey. How many men, how far, whose territory, what season, who might be waiting. Caravans were insured in practice by spreading shares among many investors precisely because the arithmetic was known. Declining to join a venture with poor odds was ordinary competence. What the ayah addresses is not the calculation but what the heart did with it once it had been made.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for a people gone to waste appears as a standalone word only twice in the Quran. The other occurrence is in a scene on the last day, where things that had been worshipped disown their worshippers and describe them as a people ruined. In both places the word is applied to people rather than to land.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a specific movement in the heart: from estimating an outcome to wanting it. The estimate is not criticised, and the ayah does not claim the odds were misread. What it names is the moment a forecast becomes comfortable, after which no further evidence will be examined honestly. That is presented as the point where a thought about probability turns into a thought about God, which the surah has already called the worse kind.

crossReferences.why: Names the same assumption a few ayat earlier, and calls it thinking an evil thought about God.
Records the same calculation after a reverse at Uhud, with people preoccupied by their own survival.
Shows three who stayed behind and were eventually turned back toward mercy, after the earth closed on them.

studies.applyIt: Notice a prediction you are making about something difficult, and ask whether you would be disappointed to be wrong. That is the whole test in this ayah. Being right is a small comfort, and it is a comfort we start reaching for early. If the answer is yes, hold the prediction more lightly for a week.

studies.title: Whom He Wills, Either Way
studies.meaning: A short ayah placed immediately after a hard verdict, and its effect is to reopen what had just closed. Ownership of everything is stated first, which is what makes the two verbs that follow possible rather than arbitrary. Then forgiveness and punishment are given in parallel, each with the same clause about will attached, so neither is described as the default. The closing pair of names breaks the symmetry, since the ayah ends on mercy rather than on the balance it had just drawn.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following several ayat about groups who held back from the journey toward Mecca and about what they had assumed. The surah has been severe for a stretch, and this ayah interrupts that severity without retracting it. The classical commentators note the placement rather than reporting an occasion, and read the closing names as leaving the previous verdict open at the edges.

keyTerms.note: Dominion in the sense of possession rather than of office. Placing it first makes what follows an exercise of ownership over what is owned, which is why no external standard is invoked in the rest of the ayah.

A verb of willing, attached identically to both halves of the sentence. Its repetition is what makes the two outcomes parallel, and the commentators are careful to read it alongside the names that close the ayah.
An intensive form from a root meaning to cover over, as a helmet covers the head. Forgiveness in this vocabulary is a shielding of something rather than a declaration that it never happened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pardon was a recognised act with a known shape. A chief could remit a blood claim, a creditor could release a debt, and a victor could let a captive go, and in each case the act was public and entirely within the giver's discretion. Nobody could be compelled to it, which is exactly what made it worth something. An audience that had watched such remissions understood the structure of this ayah before its content.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of names closing this ayah, forgiving and merciful in this exact grammatical form, occurs fourteen times in the Quran, and the great majority of those occurrences are in Medinan surahs. It is one of the Book's most frequent closing formulas, and it repeatedly gives the same two words the last position after a difficult passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah balances two possibilities and then declines to leave them balanced. By ending on mercy it establishes an asymmetry that the grammar of the middle clause had not implied, and the classical tradition has consistently read this pattern as significant rather than decorative. What is preserved is that neither outcome can be claimed as owed. What is added is that only one of the two is named as a quality of the one deciding.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same two verbs about forgiving and punishing at will, in answer to a claim of special standing.
Repeats the identical construction and closes with the same two names of forgiveness and mercy.
Gives the other direction at its widest: despair not, God forgives all sins, addressed to those who went far.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have decided is beyond fixing. A relative, a former friend, a version of yourself from ten years ago. You are not being asked to change your assessment of what they did. Only to notice that you have written the ending, and that this ayah declines to write it. Hold the file open for a week.

studies.title: Let Us Come With You
studies.meaning: A second future conversation is quoted, and the trigger for it is stated exactly: when you set out toward gains that can be collected. The same people who had reasons before now have none. The ayah names what they want, which is for a decision already stated to be altered, and it names the refusal as having been made in advance rather than by the messenger on the spot. Then their reply is quoted too. You are envious of us, which converts a decision about them into a motive of yours, and the ayah closes by saying their comprehension does not go far.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The agreement made at the edge of Mecca was followed by an expedition to Khaybar, and the classical sources connect this ayah to the question of who would take part in it, saying that those who had declined the earlier journey were not to join. The terms were understood as attached to the first refusal rather than as a new judgement, which is what the ayah's phrase about God having said so before conveys.

keyTerms.note: From a root for acquiring something without a settled price, used of a windfall. The word occurs three times in the Quran, all of them in this surah, and always as a thing being counted on.
An imperative meaning to leave someone to do a thing. It is a request for permission rather than an offer of service, which is a small difference and the whole shape of what is being asked.
Envy in the strict sense: wanting another to lose what he has. The verb occurs once in the Quran, and it is spoken by people accusing rather than being accused.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expeditions in that world were funded by their outcome. Men brought their own mounts and supplies and expected a share of whatever was taken, and shares were calculated by known rules. Joining or declining was therefore a financial decision as much as anything else, made by weighing risk against likely return. A campaign with a poor outlook drew few volunteers, and one with a good outlook drew crowds who had been unavailable a month earlier.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for gains taken in a campaign occurs three times in the whole Quran and all three are in this surah, within six ayat of each other. In one place it is what people want to be included in, in another it is part of a promise, and in the third it is what has been brought forward for them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does something unusual with the timing of judgement. The verdict is not produced in response to the new request; it is said to have been issued already, which makes the request an attempt to have a settled thing reopened rather than a fresh application. That treats a decision as an event with a date. The accusation that follows shows how such a decision is usually handled instead, by finding a motive in the person who delivers it.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same refusal in an earlier setting: you will not come out with me, having been content to sit.
Names the gains promised to those who did give the pledge, a few ayat after this refusal.
Describes the same reversal of feeling once a venture turns out well, and the wish to have been present.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you are told no and reach immediately for the other person's motive. They are threatened, they never liked me, they are protecting their own. Sometimes that is right. Sit with the possibility that the no is about the thing rather than about you, for one hour, before you decide.

studies.title: You Will Be Called Again
studies.meaning: The refusal in the previous ayah is followed immediately by an opening. Those turned away from one thing are told they will be summoned to another, and the summons is placed in the future, so the door is described as still ahead of them. The people they would face are named only by strength, and the commentators differ over who is meant, offering several identifications without agreement. Two outcomes are then given for the encounter itself, and two for the response to the call, arranged so that each has its answer.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and deliberately unspecific about what lay ahead. The classical sources record several proposals for the people of great might, from the tribes of central Arabia to the empires on the peninsula's northern edge, and they record that the identification was disputed early. What the ayah itself supplies is the structure: a second call would come, and the response to it would be counted.

keyTerms.note: A passive in the future tense. The people addressed are told what will happen to them rather than instructed, which keeps the ayah a description of an opening rather than an order given now.
Force in the sense of hardness and capacity to endure. The phrase used here occurs twice in the Quran, and the other time it is a council describing its own strength to a queen.
A wage that is good, using the ordinary word for what a hired man is paid. The vocabulary is contractual rather than exalted, which suits an offer being made to people who had already refused once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in that society was not permanent but it was sticky. A man who had failed to appear when needed carried it for years, and rehabilitation was possible only through a second occasion of the same kind. Communities kept an informal ledger of who had come out and who had not. The ayah works inside that system: the way back is not an apology accepted but another summons, still to come.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing a people of great might occurs twice in the Quran. Its other occurrence is not about believers or opponents at all; it is spoken by the council of the queen of Sheba, describing themselves to her as people of strength and severe force while leaving the decision to her.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage keeps a refusal and an opening in the same breath, without softening either. Nothing is retracted about the earlier failure, and yet the future is not closed by it, which is a specific claim about how a record works. What follows is stated as a straight pair of consequences, obedience answered by a wage and turning away answered by pain, with no third possibility offered and no assurance that the second call will be easier than the first.

crossReferences.why: Carries the same phrase about people of great might, there spoken by a council about itself.
Shows a way back opened for three who had stayed behind, after the earth had closed in on them.
Immediately narrows the summons in the next ayah, setting out who is not held to it at all.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you did not show up for. Not to apologise for it again, but to ask what the second occasion would look like if it came. Most people have never worked that out, which is why the second occasion arrives and gets missed too. Name it now, while nothing is being asked of you.

studies.title: No Blame On Them
studies.meaning: Three groups are named and the same short clause is repeated for each of them rather than collapsed into a list. The blind, the lame, the sick, and the word for blame each time. Arabic would allow one negation to cover all three, so the repetition is a choice, and the effect is that each condition is exempted on its own rather than as part of a category. Then the ayah returns to the general terms it had been using, obedience answered by gardens and turning away by pain, without any transition.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed directly after a summons addressed to people who had held back without cause. The exemption arrives immediately, before anyone could read the summons as covering everybody. The same three conditions are exempted in similar wording in two other Medinan passages, which suggests the point was raised more than once as the community organised itself around a series of demanding journeys.

keyTerms.note: From a root for narrowness and being hemmed in. The word covers both the difficulty itself and the fault attached to failing under it, so removing it removes the pressure and the shame together.
A permanent condition of the leg rather than an injury of the moment. Naming it beside sickness distinguishes what a person carries always from what has come upon him this season.
The one who is ill, with no qualification of degree attached. The absence of any measure in the wording is what the commentators note, since it leaves the condition undefined rather than graded.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A journey of weeks on foot or by camel was the ordinary demand of that period, and it selected hard for physical capacity. Someone with a damaged leg or failing eyes could not keep pace across open country and would slow everyone. Such people were also the most visible members of a small town, so an exemption said aloud mattered publicly. It removed a man from a list everyone could otherwise see he was not on.
studies.didYouKnow: The same three exemptions, in the same order and with the same word for blame repeated after each, open an ayah in another Medinan surah, where the subject is not travel at all but eating in other people's houses. A third passage exempts the weak, the sick and those who cannot find the means, adding a single condition about sincerity.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exemption is stated before any of its beneficiaries have asked, which is the passage's most striking feature. Nobody in it makes a case, produces evidence, or is assessed. That treats the removal of blame as something issued rather than granted on appeal, and it sits deliberately next to a warning aimed at people whose incapacity was a story they told. The two are held apart by the ayah without either being softened.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the identical three exemptions in the same wording, before turning to an entirely different subject.
Exempts the weak, the sick and those without means, on condition of sincerity toward God and His Messenger.
States the principle underneath: God does not burden a soul beyond what it can carry.

studies.applyIt: Think about the allowance you refuse to take. A rest you have earned, help someone offered, a task you should hand on. Many people find it easier to accept an exemption for others than for themselves. This ayah issues one without waiting to be asked, and taking it is not weakness. Take one this week.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: Under The Tree
studies.meaning: The verb opening these ayat is the one for being well pleased, and it is placed in the past tense and tied to a specific moment. What follows explains the order of events. He knew what was in their hearts, then sent down calm, then gave them an outcome. Approval comes before the settling of nerves rather than after it, and the calm is described as descending rather than arising. A place is named and a tree, so the whole passage is anchored to a piece of ground that could be walked to.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The party had halted at Hudaybiyyah, short of Mecca, and a rumour reached them that an envoy sent into the city had been killed. Under a tree at that spot, those present pledged themselves one by one. The terms agreed shortly afterward disappointed many. The nearer opening promised here is usually understood as the expedition that followed, and the surah names it before it happened.

keyTerms.note: Settled satisfaction rather than a passing approval. The verb is in the past tense and attached to a named moment, so what it records is a completed act of approval rather than a standing disposition.
From a root for stillness and dwelling. In this definite form the word occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, and both times as something sent down rather than achieved.
From a root about a thing returning to its place, which also gives the word for a garment. It describes a recompense that comes back to the one who acted rather than a prize awarded.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tree that could be found again mattered in that landscape. Landmarks were few, and a solitary acacia in open country served as a meeting point, a place of shade and a reference in directions given to travellers. Agreements were made at such places precisely because they could be named afterward. Reports say that in later years the tree at this spot could no longer be identified with certainty, and that this was thought to be for the best.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for calm sent down appears twice in this surah in this exact definite form, and nowhere else in the Quran with that spelling. Both occurrences describe it coming down onto the hearts of people who were under pressure, once at the surah's opening and once here, and in neither place is anything said about their feelings changing first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence in this passage puts knowledge before consolation and both before outcome. What is approved is the state of the heart at a moment of maximum uncertainty, before anything was known about how the affair would end, and the approval is recorded as having happened then. That detaches it entirely from the result. The calm is then described as arriving from outside, which makes steadiness under pressure something received rather than mustered.

crossReferences.why: Contains the other occurrence of the same word for calm, sent down to increase faith upon faith.
Describes the same pledge in the same surah, saying it reached past the hand that received it.
Shows the same descent of calm at an earlier moment of danger, on the road out of Mecca.

studies.applyIt: Recall a time you decided something without knowing how it would turn out, and it turned out badly. The decision and the outcome are two different objects, and most of us store them as one. Separate them today for that single memory. What this passage records is approval attached to the first, at a point when the second was still unknown.

studies.title: This One Brought Forward
studies.meaning: A large promise is made and then a small instalment is pointed at inside it. Many gains are promised, and this one has been hastened for you, so what has already arrived is described as an advance against something longer. Alongside it a second thing is named that nobody had asked for: hands were held back from you. The two purposes given at the end are unexpected, since neither is about the gains themselves. One is that it serve as a sign, and the other is guidance along a straight way.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the passage about the pledge given under the tree and the nearer opening promised there. The commentators generally read the hastened gains as those of the expedition that followed the agreement, and the restraining of hands as covering the return journey from Hudaybiyyah, when a confrontation had been possible and did not occur. The classical accounts differ over which incident is meant.

keyTerms.note: To hasten something in time, to move it earlier than its term. It presents what arrived as part of a larger promise released early rather than as the promise itself being fulfilled.
To stop a hand from reaching, the verb used of withdrawing an arm or checking a blow. The phrase about hands being restrained from you occurs once in the Quran, in this ayah.

Something that points beyond itself. Naming an outcome a sign turns it from a gain into evidence, which is why the purpose clause is about what the believers would understand rather than what they would hold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade in that region ran on advances. A partner put up capital and received an early portion against a season's returns; a buyer paid something forward on a crop still in the ground; a debt could be part-settled to show good faith while the balance stood. Everyone understood the difference between an instalment and a settlement. This ayah uses that distinction exactly, and calls what has arrived the hastened part.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase in this ayah about hands being held back from you occurs only here in the Quran. The same verb appears elsewhere in the opposite direction, where a group had been told to hold back their own hands before fighting was permitted to them. The Quran uses one verb for both, so restraint is described identically whichever side it falls on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two purposes at the end reorder the whole passage. A material outcome is given, and then it is said to be for something other than itself: to function as an indication, and to move people along a road. That makes provision instrumental without making it unreal, since the gains are named and counted. It also mentions a danger that did not happen, which is a form of favour nobody can notice at the time and few remember afterward.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same verb in reverse, where people had been told to hold back their hands before fighting.
Recalls another occasion when hands stretching toward the community were held back from them.
States the promise of many gains that this ayah describes as having been brought forward in part.

studies.applyIt: List three things that did not happen to you this year. A near miss on the road, an illness that stayed mild, a conversation that could have gone badly and did not. Nobody keeps that list, because absences leave no trace. Write it once, and notice that half of what you have been given is invisible by nature.

studies.title: A Pattern That Does Not Change
studies.meaning: Three ayat move from a specific promise to a general law. First something else, not yet within their reach, already encompassed. Then a conditional about a battle that did not happen and how it would have gone, which is an unusual thing for a text to assert. The third ayah supplies the ground for that confidence, and it is not power but regularity. What is described is a way of proceeding that has already run its course before, and the last clause denies that it can be exchanged for another.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the passage about gains brought forward and hands restrained. The surah has been reinterpreting an episode that many in the community experienced as a disappointment, and these ayat extend that reinterpretation forward and backward at once, to what had not happened yet and to what had always been the case. No specific occasion is reported for them.

keyTerms.note: To surround a thing completely, as a wall surrounds a garden. It carries both knowledge and control at once, so what is beyond someone's reach is described as already enclosed rather than merely foreseen.
A path worn by repeated use, the track left by consistent practice. The phrase occurs three times in the Quran, always about a regularity in how matters have unfolded before.
Not a change within a thing but the swapping of one thing for another. The denial is therefore specific: no alternative pattern is available to be put in this one's place.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A track across open country was made by use. Where enough caravans passed, the ground compacted and the route became visible, and travellers followed it because it had worked before rather than because anyone had laid it out. Guides read such paths for a living. The word this passage uses for God's way is that word, so a regularity in events is being described the way an audience described a road.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for God's way of proceeding occurs three times in the Quran in this exact form, two of them in a single earlier surah. In two of the three, this ayah included, the same closing clause follows word for word: you will never find an exchange for God's way. Nowhere in any of them is the pattern itself described.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The claim being made is about consistency rather than about might, which is a different kind of reassurance. A power that could do anything at any moment would give no ground for expectation; what this passage offers is that the same way of proceeding has run before and cannot be exchanged. That makes the past usable. It also sets a limit on triumph, since a pattern that holds for one community holds for the next one in the same position.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about God's way among those who passed before, and denies any alteration in it.
Says the same thing at greater length: no substitution and no turning aside in the way things have gone.
Applies the pattern to earlier messengers and states that no change will be found in it.

studies.applyIt: Look back at a difficulty you have now been through more than once. Not the details, the shape: how it started, what you did, how it resolved. Most people carry three or four of these and have never written the pattern down. Do it for one, in four lines, and keep it where you will find it next time.

studies.title: Both Hands Held Back
studies.meaning: The restraint runs in both directions and the ayah says so in the same clause: their hands from you, and yours from them. That symmetry is the point, since the second half is harder to hear than the first. A place is named, and the timing is specified as after an advantage had been given, so the withholding is described at the moment when it cost something. The closing clause is about being watched, which places the restraint under observation rather than presenting it as a lucky outcome.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical accounts describe a party from Mecca coming out toward the encamped Muslims near the boundary of the sanctuary during the negotiations, being surrounded and taken, and then released without harm. The details vary between reports, and the number involved differs from one account to another. What the ayah records is the outcome: an encounter that could have become a battle and did not.

keyTerms.note: To stop a hand from reaching. The verb appears twice in this ayah with different objects, once for one side's hands and once for the other's, which makes the restraint a single act with two directions.
The word for a belly, used of the low ground of a valley. This is the only place the city is named by this name in the Quran, which elsewhere calls the same site by an older form.
From the word for a fingernail or claw, so the image is of having got a grip on something. The verb occurs once in the Quran, and it marks the moment at which the restraint becomes costly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The area around the sanctuary carried old rules that both sides recognised. Weapons were laid aside, feuds were suspended, and a man could stand beside the person who had killed his brother. Those conventions predated the message and were among the few things the two parties still shared. An encounter inside that ground was therefore governed by something older than the dispute, which is part of why release was a possible outcome.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in the Quran that names Mecca with the name the city is known by today. One other passage refers to the same place using an older form of the name, describing the first house appointed for people. Everywhere else the Quran speaks of the city by description, as the sanctuary, the town, or the mother of settlements.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attributes an absence to God, which is a difficult thing to notice and easy to leave unrecorded. Nothing happened, so there is no event to be grateful for, and the ayah supplies one. It also assigns both restraints to the same source, which removes the reading in which one side showed discipline and the other lost its nerve. The closing clause about being seen then attaches responsibility back to the people whose hands were held.

crossReferences.why: Names the restraining of hands a few ayat earlier as part of what was given alongside the gains.
Recalls another occasion when hands stretching toward the community were held back from them.
Describes God arranging what each side saw of the other so that a matter already decided would come about.

studies.applyIt: Think of a moment you had the upper hand and did not use it. A message you did not send, a point you did not make in front of other people. Nobody thanked you, because nothing happened. Give yourself the credit this ayah gives, quietly, once, and notice how rarely that account gets settled.

studies.title: Believers You Did Not Know
studies.meaning: The ayah gives the reason behind the restraint just described, and it is not a general principle. Inside the city were believing men and believing women whom the arriving party could not identify, and an attack would have harmed them without anyone intending it. The word for what would have followed names a disgrace incurred without knowledge. Then the purpose clause: so that God might admit into His mercy whom He wills. The last sentence is a conditional about separation, saying what would have followed had the two groups been distinguishable.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at Hudaybiyyah. Some in Mecca had accepted the message and concealed it, unable to leave the city and unknown to the community outside. The classical commentators identify them generally rather than by name, and read this ayah as explaining why an available advantage was not pressed. Their existence was invisible to both sides, which is precisely the situation the ayah describes.

keyTerms.note: Confined and kept from moving on, from a root about staying beside something. Used here of the sacrificial animals prevented from reaching the place they were being brought to. The word occurs once in the Quran.
To tread on something underfoot. It is the word for what happens to what lies under an advancing crowd, so the harm described is incidental and physical rather than aimed.
To be distinguished and set apart from one another. The verb occurs once in the Quran, and the whole conditional depends on it: the two groups were mixed and could not be told apart.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca in those years held people who had accepted the message and could not leave. Some lacked the means or the protection to emigrate; some were held by families; some were slaves. They kept it quiet because the city was at war with the community outside, and being known would have cost them everything. The party camped at the boundary had no way to learn who they were, and neither did the men negotiating with them.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for a group being sorted out from one another occurs only here in the Quran, and the whole ending of this ayah turns on it. The word for the offering being held back from its destination also occurs only here. Two words used nowhere else sit in a single ayah, and both of them describe things being prevented from arriving.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage gives an unexpected reason for an outcome the community had experienced as a loss. What looked like a diplomatic reverse is presented as protection for people nobody involved could see, on both sides of a line drawn through a city. That places some part of the value of a decision permanently beyond the reach of those making it. The purpose clause makes the same point about time: mercy was being extended to people whose position had not yet declared itself.

crossReferences.why: Describes those unable to emigrate from a place, and distinguishes the genuinely powerless among them.
Addresses believers who had not emigrated, and sets out what the community owed them and did not.
Records the restraint this ayah explains, hands held back on both sides in the valley of Mecca.

studies.applyIt: Think about a decision you are about to make quickly because the situation looks clear. Then ask who is in it that you cannot see. A junior person, a family member of someone involved, whoever is not in the room. You will not be able to find them. Slowing down by a day is the only answer this ayah offers.

studies.title: Zeal Against Settledness
studies.meaning: Two states are set opposite each other and both are located in the chest. On one side a heat that the ayah names twice, first by itself and then by the era it belongs to, so the emotion is given a period as its surname. On the other side something sent down from outside onto the messenger and those with him. What follows is a phrase the commentators read in several ways, the word of guardedness, and they discuss what it names without settling it. The ayah then says those given it had the better claim to it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, describing the negotiation at Hudaybiyyah. The classical accounts report objections raised over the wording of the document, including the refusal of a title and of an opening formula, and the community's difficulty in accepting terms that read as concessions. This ayah addresses the temperature of that moment on both sides, and the surah is unusually direct in naming the older Arabian ethic by name.

keyTerms.note: From the root for heat and fever, used of a man whose blood rises to defend his own. It occurs once in the Quran, and the ayah repeats it immediately in order to attach a period to it.
A name for the pre-Islamic Arabian era, built from the word for ignorance that also carries rashness. It occurs four times in the Quran, each time attached to a different failing of that period.

A phrase occurring once in the Quran, and the commentators offer several accounts of what it names without agreeing. All the readings treat it as something fastened onto them rather than produced by them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The older ethic was not a vice in that world; it was a virtue with a name. A man was expected to feel the rise of blood when his people were slighted, and poetry celebrated exactly that response. Refusing to be humiliated in a negotiation was how standing was maintained. The document at Hudaybiyyah asked one side to accept wording that looked like a slight, in front of witnesses, and to write it down.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names the pre-Islamic era four times, and each time it attaches a different failing to it: an assumption about God after a reverse, a manner of judging, a way of displaying oneself, and here a heat in the chest. The word itself is built on the same root the Quran uses for rashness as much as for not knowing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets an emotion against a state rather than against another emotion, which changes what is being asked. What is given is not a countervailing zeal but stillness, and it is described as descending rather than as being achieved by discipline. The closing clause complicates ownership. They are said to have had the better claim to what was fastened on them, so something given from outside is at the same time called theirs by right.

crossReferences.why: Names the same era for an assumption about God that surfaced among some after a setback.
Describes the same descent of calm earlier in the surah, sent into the hearts of the believers.
Sets out the alternative to hot response, and says few are granted it apart from the patient.

studies.applyIt: Notice the physical part of your next flash of indignation. Where it starts, how long it takes to arrive, what it makes you want to say. This ayah treats that heat as a real thing with a history rather than as a judgement about the situation. Watch it for thirty seconds before deciding whether it is telling you anything true.

studies.title: The Vision Was True
studies.meaning: A vision is confirmed as true at the exact moment it appeared to have failed. The party had set out on the strength of it and had been turned back at the boundary, and this ayah addresses that gap by adjusting nothing except the timing. The content of the vision is then quoted, and it is remarkably concrete: entering in safety, heads shaven or hair shortened, without fear. The two ways of ending a state of consecration are named separately, and the phrase about God willing is inside the vision rather than added to it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Before setting out, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had seen himself entering the sanctuary at Mecca, and the community understood the journey in that light. They were prevented and agreed to terms that included returning the following year. The ayah was given while the disappointment was fresh, and the entry described took place a year later under those terms.

keyTerms.note: The specific word for something seen while asleep, distinct from ordinary sight. The Quran uses it for the visions of Joseph and of Abraham, so it belongs to a small and consequential set of passages.
From the root for shaving. It occurs once in the Quran, and it names one of the two ways a state of consecration is brought to an end, the other being named immediately after it.

Secure, from the root that also gives the words for faith and for trustworthiness. Its presence in the vision is what the following clause returns to, since the entry is described twice as being without fear.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Entering the sanctuary in a state of consecration had a visible protocol that everyone in the region knew. Pilgrims wore unsewn cloth, avoided cutting hair or nails, and brought animals marked with garlands so that anyone could see they were bound for the shrine. Ending that state by shaving or shortening the hair was public and unmistakable. The party at Hudaybiyyah performed that ending short of the city, in the open, and then turned home.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about God willing appears inside the quoted vision itself rather than as a comment on it. Classical commentators discuss why a statement being confirmed as true should carry that qualification, and their answers range from it being part of what was seen to it being the way certainty about the future is properly expressed even when the outcome is guaranteed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates truth from timing and insists on both. The vision is called true without qualification, and the events that seemed to contradict it are left standing, so the resolution is not that the community misread the dream but that they supplied a date for it. The clause about knowing what they did not know then generalises this. The gap between a promise and its arrival is filled by information that was never available to the people waiting.

crossReferences.why: Gives another vision that took decades to arrive, and was recognised only when its meaning came about.
Shows the fulfilment of that earlier vision, named as such by the one who had seen it as a boy.
Describes what is done when a journey to the sanctuary is prevented, including the offering and the hair.

studies.applyIt: Take something you were sure of that did not happen when you expected. Before deciding you were wrong, try adding a date to it and see whether the sentence still stands. Most disappointment is a timing error read as a content error, and the two feel identical from inside the week they happen in.

studies.title: Sent With Guidance And Truth
studies.meaning: A single sentence appears three times in the Quran, and this is one of the three. The sending is described by what accompanied it, guidance and a way of life characterised by truth, and then by a purpose clause. The verb in that clause is discussed at length by the commentators, who read it as making something manifest, or uppermost, or clear against alternatives, and they differ over whether what is described is argument, historical spread, or something not yet arrived. The closing clause is short and unusually restrained: God suffices as witness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the section of the surah about the agreement at the boundary. The community had just accepted terms that read at the time as a reverse, and the surah has spent several ayat resetting the frame. This sentence arrives at that point and is also found in two other surahs, one earlier and one later, in each case attached to a different immediate situation.

keyTerms.note: The first word covers a way of life, an obligation, and a reckoning all at once. Joining it to truth describes a whole ordering of life by its correspondence to what is real rather than by its origin.

keyTerms.gloss: that He may make it manifest
keyTerms.note: From a root for a back or an outer surface, so the verb means to bring something to the outside. The commentators read it variously as becoming clear, becoming uppermost, or being made known, and they do not agree.

The legal word for one whose testimony settles a matter. Ending a claim about the future with a witness rather than with a guarantee places the assurance in someone's testimony rather than in a schedule.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia in that period contained many ways of ordering a life, and people knew the map. There were Jewish and Christian communities with their own scriptures and calendars, older Arabian practice centred on shrines, and individuals remembered as having withdrawn from all of it to seek something else. A claim that one of these would become manifest was not made into a vacuum; it was made among neighbours who had chosen differently.
studies.didYouKnow: This sentence appears three times in the Quran in nearly identical wording, in three different surahs. Two of the three continue with a clause about those who set up rivals to God disliking it; this one does not, ending instead with the shortest of the three closings. The variation between them is a single clause in each case.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah says nothing about how or by whom the purpose is to be achieved, which is a significant silence given the setting. It names a sending and an intention and then stops, and the classical readings differ over whether what is described belongs to evidence, to history, or to a time still ahead. What it does say is that the confirming testimony is God's, which places the whole claim beyond what any community could demonstrate on its own behalf.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same sentence, followed by a clause about those who associate partners disliking it.
Repeats it a third time, alongside the image of trying to put out a light with the mouth.
Places a boundary around any spread of the way: no compulsion, since guidance stands clear of error.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you would accept as evidence that something you believe is true. Not proof to convince anyone else, just what would count for you. Most people have never answered that question about anything important. Write one sentence for one belief today, and notice how the question changes the belief a little.

studies.title: Stern Outside, Tender Within
studies.meaning: The ayah gives a portrait rather than a rule. A pair of dispositions is set side by side: firmness outward and mercy among themselves. The same people are then shown bowing and prostrating, seeking nothing but God's favour. Scholars differ over the mark on the faces. Some read it as a physical trace of prostration, some as a light visible in the features, some as a sign appearing on the Day of Resurrection. The closing image is from farming: a shoot that thickens until it stands on its own stem.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It is the closing ayah of a surah that came down after the truce agreed outside Mecca, in the sixth year after the emigration. It names the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) directly, which the Quran rarely does. The community described was roughly fifteen years old and still small enough to count. The reference to descriptions in the Torah and the Gospel addresses an audience in Medina that included readers of both.

keyTerms.note: A plural from the root behind mercy and the word for a womb. Set against sternness in the same breath, it describes not politeness but the protectiveness of shared blood, extended to people who are not kin.

A word for a distinguishing feature by which a thing is recognised, used of horses branded for a stable. It names something visible to an observer rather than something felt by the one who carries it.

The small offshoot a plant throws out beside the main stalk. The parable begins with the least impressive part of the plant, and the strengthening described is the shoot supporting the parent rather than the reverse.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was farmland. Date palms and barley grew in the volcanic soil around the settlement, and everyone knew what a young crop looked like in the weeks when it could still fail. A field that came through that stage stood up all at once and could be seen from a distance. Farmers took open pleasure in it, which is exactly the word the ayah uses, and the pleasure was as much relief as pride.
studies.didYouKnow: The Prophet is called by name only four times in the whole Quran. This ayah is the last of them in the order of the Book. Elsewhere he is addressed by title, as messenger or prophet or simply as you. A fifth passage, in surah 61, gives a different form of the same name. It is reported there as the announcement made by Jesus.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage defines a community by character, not by a belief stated or a line drawn. Two of the qualities named point in a direction. The same person is described as hard one way and soft another. The tradition reads that pairing as one character, not as a contradiction. The parable then makes growth slow and living. That places the community's spread outside anyone's control, including its own.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same paired disposition as a description of a people God will bring, humble within and firm without.
Contains the passage referred to here, an announcement of the coming messenger placed on the lips of Jesus.
Explains the inward gentleness from the other side, saying harshness would have scattered the same community.

studies.applyIt: Notice which direction your firmness points this week. Most people find they are stern with the people closest to them, and easy-going with everyone else. That is the exact reverse of the portrait here. Pick one person in your household or your circle. Give them the benefit of the doubt once, on something small, without mentioning that you did.
studies.explainEasier: The people with God's messenger are firm with those who fight them and kind to each other. You see them bowing and kneeling, hoping for God's blessing. They grow like a young plant that gets strong and stands on its own.
